God has bound Himself by His word, and “all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Our obedience does not purchase blessing; it places us where God has promised to bless.

Likewise, decreeing a thing is not a magic formula for commanding God. It is speaking and praying in line with His will, for “if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us” (1 John 5:14). Notice the condition in Job 22:30: deliverance comes “by the pureness of thine hands”. Bold declarations must come from honest lives.
When faithful people suffer

God’s blessing is not always money or ease. It includes peace, a good name, children who walk in truth and His presence in trouble. Hebrews 11 lists heroes of faith who escaped the sword, and others, just as faithful, who were mocked, imprisoned and killed, and says “these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise” in their lifetime (Hebrews 11:39). Job himself suffered greatly while being righteous. So never assume that a struggling family is cursed, and never promise that faith guarantees wealth. God’s blessing is certain, but its form and timing belong to Him.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Keep sowing love and honesty even when the harvest seems slow. God has not forgotten.
Practical steps

items: Pray God’s promises over your family in line with His will, but check first that your hands are clean in the matter you are praying about.
Choose one way this month for your family’s blessing to reach beyond your home: your street, your church or a colleague in need.
When a faithful family you know is suffering, visit, pray and help rather than suspecting them.

blocks.text: Questions for reflection

items: Why is it important to know who spoke Job 22:28-30, and how does the rest of Scripture support its principle?
How has God’s blessing on one faithful person overflowed to others in your experience?
What is the difference between trusting God’s promises and trying to force God?
How would you encourage a faithful family that is going through hardship?

sections.title: Point 13: The Thin Line Between Love of Money and Love of God

blocks.text:
13. FINALLY: There is a thin line between LOVE OF MONEY AND LOVE OF GOD.
1. Love of money is the root of all evil and those who love it will perish. Proverbs 11:28.
2. Love of God is the root of all blessings.

The leaflet closes with the word “Finally”, and its last warning is about money. This is no change of subject. Points 5 to 9 asked why a praying, richly blessed nation is known for corruption. Much of the answer lies here: when money is loved more than God, love for neighbour gives way to bribes, fraud and neglect of the family. The leaflet sets two roots side by side and asks every home which one it is growing from.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.

Money itself is not evil; it is the love of money that Paul condemns. Many readers understand this verse to mean that the love of money is a root from which every kind of evil can grow. Paul wrote it while warning against people who supposed “that gain is godliness” (1 Timothy 6:5) and reminding Timothy that “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6).
He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch.

The leaflet cites this proverb to support its warning that those who love money will perish. Love of money shows itself as trust in riches – treating money as security, protection and saviour. Such a person “shall fall”, whether suddenly or slowly. The righteous, by contrast, “flourish as a branch”, drawing life from a root they did not create. That is the leaflet’s second statement in picture form: the love of God is the root from which true blessing grows.
Why the line is thin
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.

From the outside, a person who loves God and a person who loves money can look alike. Both work hard, pray for provision and give in church. The difference is in the heart: which one is master? “Mammon” means wealth treated as a lord. You may have crossed the line when you are willing to lie or compromise for money, when family time is always sacrificed for income, when you measure people by what they have, when you give in order to be seen or to “buy” a blessing, or when anxiety about money rules your home.
Where the line is crossed in homes

**Marriage.** Bride price and wedding customs can honour families and bring them together. But when negotiations become a sale, when a daughter is valued by what she will bring, or when a couple begins marriage buried in debt for the sake of display, love of money has entered the home before the marriage has begun.

**Children’s education.** Every parent wants the best for their children. The line is crossed when parents borrow beyond their means to impress other parents with a school’s name, push a child into a course only for the money it may bring, or are so busy earning school fees that no one is raising the child.

**The “Nigerian factor”.** Paying to jump a queue, inflating a receipt, “settling” an official, or using church connections to win contracts are often excused with the words “that is how things work here”. Scripture warns, “the gift blindeth the wise” (Exodus 23:8), and “He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27). Many families face real economic pressure, and choosing honesty can be costly. God sees that cost.
The root of all blessings
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.

In the King James Version, “conversation” means your whole way of life. Contentment is not laziness; it is freedom from the fear that God will not provide. Paul told the rich to “do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute” (1 Timothy 6:18), and told former thieves to work so that they “may have to give to him that needeth” (Ephesians 4:28). When God is loved first, money becomes a servant of love.
Practical steps

items: Husband and wife: be open with each other about income, spending and debts.
Agree on family money rules: no dishonest income, no bribes, and regular giving to God and to people in need.
Teach children to earn, save and give, and explain why you refuse shortcuts.
Keep family time protected, even in busy seasons of work.

blocks.text: Questions for reflection

items: What signs might show that money has become a master in your home?
How does Proverbs 11:28 help explain the difference between love of money and love of God?
Which of the areas above – marriage, education, or the “Nigerian factor” – is the greatest temptation for your family?
What would seeking first the kingdom of God look like in your family’s finances this month?

blocks.text: When God is loved first, money becomes a servant of love.

The teaching of this leaflet is meant to be lived, not only studied. Gather your household, read the prayer together, and talk through the commitments. Parents may wish to write the list in a notebook and let each family member sign it, then review it together once a month. Adapt the words to fit your household – for example, where a parent is raising children alone, or where grandparents or other relatives share your home.
A family prayer

Heavenly Father, we thank You that You first loved us and gave Your Son for us. We confess that our family has not always loved You with all our heart, nor loved one another as we should. Forgive us for harsh words, grudges, lies, favouritism and the love of money. Pour Your love into our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

Teach the husband in this home to love his wife as Christ loved the church, and the wife to love her husband. Help us as parents to love our children with patience and wise correction, and help our children to honour and love their parents. Make us humble enough to hear one another, and make our home a church where Your word is spoken, prayer is made and strangers are welcomed.

Let Your blessing on our home overflow to our church, our neighbours, our places of work and our nation. Heal Nigeria, Lord, and let righteousness begin with us. Keep us from loving money more than You. We ask this in the name of Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.
Our family commitment

items: We will love God first, and keep a regular time of family devotion.
We will practise one quality of love from 1 Corinthians 13 each week.
We will not keep grudges, but will seek to forgive and be reconciled quickly.
We will speak the truth at home and outside, and refuse bribes and dishonest shortcuts.
As parents, we will listen when our family members assess us, and we will correct our children without harshness or abuse.
We will treat every person in our home, including relatives and house helps, with dignity and fairness.
We will open our home for prayer and hospitality, and support our local church.
We will record and share God’s faithfulness to our family truthfully.
We will seek first the kingdom of God and use our money to serve love.

blocks.text: Charity begins at home – and from home it reaches the nation.
